chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad, raising it (with a gap in the chain), from Muhammad ibn al-Faraj al-Rukhkhaji, who said:
I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him about what Hisham ibn al-Hakam said regarding [Allah's] body (jism), and what Hisham ibn Salim said regarding [Allah's] image (sura).
So he wrote: 'Leave from yourself the confusion of the confused ones, and seek refuge with God from Satan. The correct saying is not what the two Hishams have spoken.'

key_terms.الجسم: jism — body, corporeal substance; used in kalam to debate God's corporeality
key_terms.الصورة: sura — image, form, shape; Hisham ibn Salim's concept of God having a form
key_terms.الهشامان: al-Hishamani — the two Hishams; dual form referring to Hisham ibn al-Hakam and Hisham ibn Salim, both theologians in Imam al-Sadiq's circle
key_terms.حَيْرَةَ الْحَيْرَانِ: hayrat al-hayran — the confusion of the confused ones; a rhetorical expression dismissing anthropomorphic theology as spiritual bewilderment

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Hadi say about Hisham ibn al-Hakam's view that God has a body?
ai.summary: The Imam al-Hadi (peace be upon him) received a letter from Muhammad ibn al-Faraj al-Rukhkhaji inquiring about the theological positions of two prominent Shia scholars — Hisham ibn al-Hakam, who had argued that God possesses a body (jism), and Hisham ibn Salim, who had argued that God has a form or image (sura). The Imam responded decisively in writing, rejecting both positions as confusion leading the believer astray, warning that such anthropomorphic descriptions of God belong to the domain of Satan's temptations. This hadith is one of several in this chapter that establish the Imami creedal position: God transcends all physical attributes, whether body, form, or image. The two Hishams were figures within the Shia theological school (kalam) who used Greek philosophical categories, but the Imam's response indicates that such speculative attempts to define God's nature overstep the limits of correct belief.
